At midnight, the last bus to Crosstown carried six sleepy passengers, a bouquet of lilies, and one enormous watermelon wrapped in newspaper for her breakfast. The driver, Nadia, knew every routine: the nurse ending her shift, the student with paint beneath his fingernails, the old man singing softly to himself.

She also knew their secrets, though none belonged to her: an apology rehearsed at every stop, a lottery ticket folded into a very tiny square. At the final stop, the student woke, gathered his things, and left the lilies beside the driver without a word. Nadia pretended not to notice.

By morning, the bouquet rested in a station café, brightening a chipped blue vase between two glasses of black coffee left there by a mystery. The nurse returned that afternoon, purchased a single white rose, and wondered why the florist kept smiling. Perhaps she had caught something good from elsewhere.

The old man missed his stop, slept through his alarm, and woke in a neighborhood he had never seen before. He smiled without knowing why. Later, he told everyone that the city had rearranged itself specifically for him, which was probably not true. But he bought coffee for strangers there.

By sunset, Nadia discovered the watermelon had survived the ride, somehow unharmed beneath those patient, borrowed newspaper pages. She repacked it, wondering about its owner.

Some gifts travel badly, some arrive too late, and some, like kindness, seem to know exactly where they are going. Even when nobody sends them.
